title: Corollary: no offense is venial of itself—only relative to mercy
source_text: XIV. Postea vero ex ista conclusione plura corollaria deducit, quorum hoc primum est; Nulla offensa Dei est venialis de se, nisi tantummodo per respectum ad divinam misericordiam, quae non vult de facto quamlibet offensam imputare ad mortem, cum istud posset justissime. Et ita concluditur quod peccatum mortale & veniale, in esse tali non distinguuntur intrinsece & essentialiter, sed solum per respectum ad divinam gratiam, quae peccatum istud imputat ad poenam mortis, & aliud non.
pass_a_gloss: Afterwards, moreover, from that conclusion he deduces several corollaries, of which this is the first: No offense of God is venial of itself, except only by respect to the divine mercy, which does not will in fact to impute every offense unto death, although it could most justly do so. And so it is concluded that mortal and venial sin, in being such, are not distinguished intrinsically and essentially, but only by respect to the divine grace which imputes this sin to the punishment of death and not the other.
pass_b_english: Gerson’s first corollary: nothing is venial of itself—only because mercy declines to impute every offense unto death.
Mortal and venial then differ not by essence but by how grace imputes penalty.
